# Who this article is for

You know `brms`. You have written `brm(y ~ x + (1 | id))`, read its summary, and
perhaps written a non-linear formula or two. Then you open a `bmm` article and
the formula has no response on its left-hand side, the model is an object of its
own, and the estimates come with links you did not choose. This article
translates between the two packages.

We fit one model twice: once in plain `brms`, once with `bmm`. The model is the
two-parameter mixture model for continuous reproduction tasks
[@Zhang_Luck_2008], which `brms` can express with its built-in mixture family.
Both fits run the same Stan model, so they give the same estimates. With that
established, the rest of the article explains each difference in the code: where
the response went, why every parameter gets its own formula, what
`0 + setsize` and `1 + setsize` each give you, which scale the estimates are on,
and why `bmm` sets informative default priors. A later section does the same
comparison for signal detection:
[trial-level `sdt_yn()` against a probit generalized linear mixed model](#signal-detection-as-a-probit-glmm).

# The same model, written twice

## The data

`zhang_luck_2008` ships with `bmm`. Eight participants saw one, two, three or
six colored squares, and after a delay they reproduced the color of one of them
on a color wheel. The response error is the distance between the reported and
the true color, in radians:

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(bmm)
library(brms)

dat <- zhang_luck_2008
head(dat[, c("subID", "setsize", "response_error")])
```

`setsize` is a factor. With a numeric column, `0 + setsize` below would fit a
single slope instead of one value per set size.

The mixture model assumes that a response comes either from memory or from a
guess. Memory responses scatter around the true color with a von Mises
distribution, the normal distribution of the circle, whose precision is `kappa`.
Guesses fall anywhere on the circle with equal probability. The second parameter
is the probability that a response comes from memory. We let both parameters
differ between set sizes and between participants.

## The model in brms

In `brms`, this is a mixture of two von Mises distributions. Each component has
a location (`mu1`, `mu2`) and a precision (`kappa1`, `kappa2`), and `theta1` is
the weight of the first component. Turning this into the mixture model takes
three constraints. Both locations are fixed at 0, because the response error is
already relative to the target. The precision of the second component is fixed
at a value so small that the distribution is flat, which makes it the guessing
distribution. Constant priors do the fixing:

```{r brms-fit, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
brms_fit <- brm(
  formula = bf(
    response_error ~ 1,
    kappa1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    theta1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    mu2 ~ 1,
    kappa2 ~ 1
  ),
  family = mixture(von_mises, von_mises, order = "none"),
  prior = prior(constant(0), class = Intercept, dpar = mu1) +
    prior(constant(0), class = Intercept, dpar = mu2) +
    prior(constant(-100), class = Intercept, dpar = kappa2) +
    prior(normal(2, 1), class = b, dpar = kappa1) +
    prior(logistic(0, 1), class = b, dpar = theta1) +
    prior(exponential(1), class = sd, dpar = kappa1) +
    prior(exponential(1), class = sd, dpar = theta1),
  data = dat,
  cores = 4,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "assets/brmsfit_brms_to_bmm"
)
```

`kappa2` is fixed at -100 because `brms` estimates `kappa` on the log scale, and
`exp(-100)` is as close to zero as anyone needs. At the default `adapt_delta`
of 0.8, the sampler occasionally reports a divergent transition for this model,
so we raise it; this is a `brms` argument and works the same in `bmm()`.
`file =` saves the fit and loads it on later runs instead of refitting, so
change the name, or drop the argument, when you change the data or the model.
The last four priors are not the `brms` defaults. They are the priors `bmm`
uses for this model, and we pass them here so that both fits are the same model.
We come back to them in
[the section on priors](#why-the-default-priors-are-informative).

## The model in bmm

The `bmm` version needs a model object, one formula per parameter, and the data:

```{r bmm-fit, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
bmm_fit <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    kappa ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    thetat ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID)
  ),
  data = dat,
  model = mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error"),
  cores = 4,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "assets/bmmfit_brms_to_bmm"
)
```

The constraints are gone from the code. `mixture2p()` knows that the locations
are 0, that the second component is the guessing distribution, and which priors
to use. What is left is what you want to know: how `kappa` and `thetat`, the
weight of the memory responses (the `t` stands for target), depend on set size.

## Same model, same estimates

`bmm` translates its formula into a `brmsformula`, and `brms` writes the Stan
model from that. You can look at the formula `bmm` generated:

```{r}
bmm_fit$formula
```

`kappa` and `thetat` are non-linear parameters that `bmm` passes on to `kappa1`
and `theta1`. `mu1`, `mu2` and `kappa2` are fixed with constant priors, as in
the `brms` call. Apart from the parameter names, the Stan code of the two fits
is the same program with the same priors, so the posteriors agree up to the
noise of the sampler. Both columns are on the link scale, log `kappa` and logit
`thetat`, which we explain [below](#which-scale-the-estimates-are-on):

```{r, message = FALSE}
brms_est <- fixef(brms_fit)
bmm_est <- fixef(bmm_fit)
ci <- function(est, row) {
  sprintf(
    "%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]",
    est[row, "Estimate"], est[row, "Q2.5"], est[row, "Q97.5"]
  )
}
set_sizes <- levels(dat$setsize)
comparison <- data.frame(
  parameter = rep(c("kappa", "thetat"), each = length(set_sizes)),
  set_size = rep(set_sizes, 2),
  brms = c(
    sapply(paste0("kappa1_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = brms_est),
    sapply(paste0("theta1_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = brms_est)
  ),
  bmm = c(
    sapply(paste0("kappa_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = bmm_est),
    sapply(paste0("thetat_setsize", set_sizes), ci, est = bmm_est)
  )
)
knitr::kable(comparison, row.names = FALSE)
```

For this model, `bmm` adds nothing to the Stan program. It writes the `brms`
code, checks the data, and picks priors and starting values that suit the
model. For models that `brms` has no family for, such as `sdm()` or
`cswald()`, `bmm` also supplies the Stan code of the likelihood.

# Where the response lives

In `brms`, the response is on the left-hand side of the main formula:
`response_error ~ 1`. In `bmm`, it is an argument of the model object:
`mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error")`. The formulas only ever have
parameters on their left-hand side.

The reason is that a measurement model usually needs more than one column, and
each column plays a different role. The three-parameter mixture model needs the
response error, the colors of the items that were not cued, and the set size.
A yes/no signal detection model needs the number of "old" responses, the number
of trials, and whether the item was old or new. In `brms`, these roles end up
spread over the response, addition terms such as `| trials()`, and predictors
inside non-linear formulas. In `bmm`, the model object names each column once,
by its role:

```r
mixture3p(
  resp_error = "response_error", nt_features = "col_lure",
  set_size = "setsize", regex = TRUE
)
sdt_yn(response = "n_old", stimulus = "stimulus", n_trials = "n_trials")
```

Knowing the role of each column lets `bmm` check the data before anything is
compiled. For instance, `mixture2p()` warns if the response error looks like
degrees rather than radians. It also lets `bmm` build the columns that the Stan
model needs from the ones you have, such as which of the non-target columns are
filled at each set size. The help page of each model, such as `?mixture2p`,
lists the columns it expects.

# Signal detection as a probit GLMM

Many psychologists already fit signal detection models without calling them
that. With one row per trial, `resp` coded 1 for an "old" response and
`stimulus` coded 1 for a studied item and 0 for a new one, a yes/no recognition
experiment is often analyzed as a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a
probit link:

```r
brm(
  resp ~ 0 + Intercept + stimulus + (1 + stimulus | id) + (1 + stimulus | item),
  family = bernoulli("probit")
)
```

This is the equal-variance Gaussian signal detection model [@DeCarlo_1998]. In
`bmm`, the same model is `sdt_yn()` with one row per trial: leave out
`n_trials`, and `response` holds the 0 or 1 of each trial.

## How the parameters map

The probability of an "old" response is `pnorm(Intercept)` for a new item and
`pnorm(Intercept + stimulus)` for a studied one, where `stimulus` stands for its
coefficient. In signal detection terms, these are `pnorm(-criterion)` and
`pnorm(d - criterion)`: the evidence of a new item is normal with mean 0 and
standard deviation (SD) 1, that of a studied item normal with mean `d`, and the
participant says "old" when the evidence lies above the criterion. The
criterion is thus measured from the mean of the new items. Matching the two
pairs of probabilities gives the intercept as minus the criterion and the
`stimulus` coefficient as `d`. So each part of the `brms` model has a `bmm`
name:

| `bmm` (`sdt_yn()`) | `brms` probit GLMM |
|---|---|
| `d` | coefficient of `stimulus` |
| `criterion` | minus the intercept |
| `(1 \| id)` in the formula of `d` | `stimulus` slope by `id` |
| `(1 \| id)` in the formula of `criterion` | intercept by `id` |
| `(1 \| item)` in the formula of `d` | `stimulus` slope by `item` |
| `(1 \| item)` in the formula of `criterion` | intercept by `item` |
| `sdratio` (unequal variance) | none: the probit GLMM fixes both standard deviations at 1 |
| `bias` (criterion measured from the midpoint between the two distributions) | minus the intercept if `stimulus` is coded -0.5 / +0.5; with the 0 / 1 coding used here, `-(Intercept + stimulus / 2)` |
| `dist` (the distribution of the evidence) | partly: `bernoulli("logit")` is `dist = "logistic"` and `bernoulli("cloglog")` is `dist = "gumbel_max"`; no link gives `dist = "gumbel_min"` for a response coded 1 = "old" (see below the table) |

In the `dist` row, the link is that of the probability of an "old" response,
whereas `?sdt_yn` gives each `dist` by the cumulative distribution function of
the evidence. The function `1 - exp(-exp(x))`, the inverse of the complementary
log-log link, is listed there under `"gumbel_min"`; the probability of "old"
under `"gumbel_max"` is that same function of `d - criterion`. With the response
coded 1 for "new" instead, `bernoulli("cloglog")` gives `dist = "gumbel_min"`:
the probability of "new" is that function of `criterion - d * stimulus`.

`stimulus` itself appears in no `bmm` formula: it is named in the model object,
`sdt_yn(stimulus = "stimulus")`, and `d` is its effect, so a predictor in the
formula of `d` is always one that interacts with `stimulus`. A predictor of the
`brms` intercept is a predictor of `criterion`, with its sign flipped, and its
interaction with `stimulus` is a predictor of `d`. For a design factor `cond`,
`resp ~ 0 + Intercept + stimulus * cond` is `bmf(d ~ 1 + cond, criterion ~ 1 + cond)`.
The `d` coefficients are the `stimulus` and `stimulus:cond` coefficients, and
the `criterion` coefficients are the intercept and `cond` coefficients, each
multiplied by -1.

The intercept by participant changes sign along with the intercept, so its
SD is the SD of the criterion. Beyond the parameters, `bmm` adds helpers for the
receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and the area under the ROC curve (AUC),
which the
[signal detection article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_sdt.html)
describes.

## Both fits on one data set

To check the mapping, we simulate a recognition experiment in which 30
participants each see the same 60 items. Half of the participants studied
items 1 to 30, the other half items 31 to 60, so every item is old for 15
participants and new for the other 15. `d` and `criterion` vary between
participants and between items. The data come from the latent normal
distributions of the model directly, not from a `bmm` function, so that the
check does not depend on `bmm`'s own code:

```{r glmm-data}
set.seed(4646)
truth <- c(
  d = 1.3, criterion = 0.6,
  sd_id_d = 0.4, sd_id_criterion = 0.25,
  sd_item_d = 0.3, sd_item_criterion = 0.2
)
n_id <- 30
n_item <- 60
rec <- expand.grid(id = seq_len(n_id), item = seq_len(n_item))
rec$stimulus <- as.integer((rec$item <= n_item / 2) == (rec$id %% 2 == 1))

id_d <- rnorm(n_id, 0, truth[["sd_id_d"]])
id_criterion <- rnorm(n_id, 0, truth[["sd_id_criterion"]])
item_d <- rnorm(n_item, 0, truth[["sd_item_d"]])
item_criterion <- rnorm(n_item, 0, truth[["sd_item_criterion"]])
trial_d <- truth[["d"]] + id_d[rec$id] + item_d[rec$item]
trial_criterion <- truth[["criterion"]] + id_criterion[rec$id] +
  item_criterion[rec$item]

# new items draw their evidence from normal(0, 1), old items from normal(d, 1)
evidence <- rnorm(nrow(rec), mean = rec$stimulus * trial_d)
rec$resp <- as.integer(evidence > trial_criterion)
rec$id <- factor(rec$id)
rec$item <- factor(rec$item)
head(rec)
```

```{r glmm-priors-check, include = FALSE}
sdt_priors <- sdt_yn(response = "resp", stimulus = "stimulus")$default_priors
# the brms chunk hard-codes these defaults, the criterion's with its sign flipped
if (!identical(
  c(sdt_priors$d$main, sdt_priors$criterion$main, sdt_priors$d$sd,
    sdt_priors$criterion$sd),
  c("normal(1, 1)", "normal(0.5, 1.5)", "exponential(1)", "exponential(1)")
)) {
  stop("The sdt_yn default priors changed: revise the brms GLMM chunk.")
}
```

The `brms` fit is the GLMM from above. As in the first example, we give it the
priors that `bmm` uses for `sdt_yn()`, so that the priors on the means and the
SDs agree. `?sdt_yn` lists them: `r sdt_priors$d$main` on `d`,
`r sdt_priors$criterion$main` on `criterion` and `r sdt_priors$d$sd` on every
SD. On the intercept, the criterion's prior has its sign flipped:

```{r glmm-brms-fit, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
glmm_fit <- brm(
  resp ~ 0 + Intercept + stimulus + (1 + stimulus | id) + (1 + stimulus | item),
  family = bernoulli("probit"),
  prior = prior(normal(-0.5, 1.5), class = b, coef = Intercept) +
    prior(normal(1, 1), class = b, coef = stimulus) +
    prior(exponential(1), class = sd),
  data = rec,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 646,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "fits/brmsfit_sdt_glmm_brms_to_bmm"
)
```

The `bmm` fit names the two columns in `sdt_yn()` and gives `d` and
`criterion` a formula each:

```{r glmm-bmm-fit, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
trial_fit <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    d ~ 1 + (1 | id) + (1 | item),
    criterion ~ 1 + (1 | id) + (1 | item)
  ),
  data = rec,
  model = sdt_yn(response = "resp", stimulus = "stimulus"),
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 646,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "fits/bmmfit_sdt_trial_brms_to_bmm"
)
```

`stimulus` appears in neither formula. `sdt_yn()` reads it from the column
named in the model object and uses it to decide whether `d` enters a trial, the
job that the `stimulus` predictor does in `brms`. The `1` in `d ~ 1` is the
population `d`, the coefficient of `stimulus` in the GLMM, and `(1 | id)` lets
it vary between participants, as the `stimulus` slope by `id` does.

The fits still differ in the correlations. `(1 + stimulus | id)` in `brms` also
estimates the correlation between each participant's intercept and slope, and
the same for items. The `bmm` formula above leaves these correlations out.
Write `(1 + stimulus || id)` to drop them in `brms`, or give the participant
terms of `d` and `criterion` a shared ID, `(1 | p | id)`, to add them in `bmm`.
The `bmm` correlation is that of `d` and `criterion`, which is minus the `brms`
correlation of slope and intercept, because the intercept is minus the
criterion. The default priors on a correlation also differ: `brms` uses
LKJ(1) and `bmm` uses LKJ(2): `make_stancode()` of the `brms` model shows
LKJ(1), and `stancode()` of a `bmm` model with `(1 | p | id)` shows LKJ(2).
`prior(lkj(2), class = cor)` gives the `brms` model the `bmm` prior.

The table puts the estimates of the two fits next to the values we simulated
from, each as the posterior mean and its 95% credible interval (CrI). The
`brms` intercept and its draws are multiplied by -1 to give the criterion:

```{r glmm-compare}
glmm_draws <- as_draws_df(glmm_fit)
trial_draws <- as_draws_df(trial_fit)
glmm_par <- list(
  d = glmm_draws$b_stimulus,
  criterion = -glmm_draws$b_Intercept,
  sd_id_d = glmm_draws$sd_id__stimulus,
  sd_id_criterion = glmm_draws$sd_id__Intercept,
  sd_item_d = glmm_draws$sd_item__stimulus,
  sd_item_criterion = glmm_draws$sd_item__Intercept
)
trial_par <- list(
  d = trial_draws$b_d_Intercept,
  criterion = trial_draws$b_criterion_Intercept,
  sd_id_d = trial_draws$sd_id__d_Intercept,
  sd_id_criterion = trial_draws$sd_id__criterion_Intercept,
  sd_item_d = trial_draws$sd_item__d_Intercept,
  sd_item_criterion = trial_draws$sd_item__criterion_Intercept
)
mean_cri <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975))
  sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", mean(x), q[1], q[2])
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  parameter = c("d", "criterion", "SD of d by id", "SD of criterion by id",
                "SD of d by item", "SD of criterion by item"),
  `brms term` = c("stimulus", "-Intercept", "sd(stimulus) by id",
                  "sd(Intercept) by id", "sd(stimulus) by item",
                  "sd(Intercept) by item"),
  simulated = truth[names(glmm_par)],
  brms = vapply(glmm_par, mean_cri, character(1)),
  bmm = vapply(trial_par, mean_cri, character(1)),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r glmm-agreement, include = FALSE}
inside <- function(x, draws) {
  q <- quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.975))
  mean(x) >= q[1] && mean(x) <= q[2]
}
mutual <- mapply(function(a, b) inside(a, b) && inside(b, a), glmm_par, trial_par)
if (!all(mutual)) {
  stop("brms and bmm disagree on: ", paste(names(glmm_par)[!mutual], collapse = ", "))
}
largest_gap <- max(abs(vapply(glmm_par, mean, numeric(1)) -
                         vapply(trial_par, mean, numeric(1))))
covered <- function(par) {
  mapply(function(x, draws) {
    q <- quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.975))
    x >= q[1] && x <= q[2]
  }, truth[names(par)], par)
}
# the text before the chunk states the design as numbers
if (n_id != 30 || n_item != 60) {
  stop("n_id or n_item changed: revise '30 participants', '60 items', ",
       "'items 1 to 30', '31 to 60' and '15 participants' in the text above.")
}
# the text says every simulated value lies inside both intervals
if (!all(covered(glmm_par), covered(trial_par))) {
  stop("A simulated value lies outside a 95% CrI: revise the text under the table.")
}
```

For every row, each fit's estimate lies inside the other fit's 95% CrI, and
the two estimates differ by at most `r sprintf("%.2f", largest_gap)`. Every
simulated value lies inside both intervals. The intervals of the SDs are wide,
because `r n_id` participants and `r n_item` items are few groups from which to
estimate a spread.

## The item effects on `d`

The item SD of `d` rests on fewer trials than the item SD of the criterion.
On a trial with a new item, `d` does not enter the probability of an "old"
response, `pnorm(-criterion)`, so an item's effect on `d` is estimated only
from the trials on which the item was old: `r n_id / 2` per item here, against
`r n_id` for its effect on the criterion. The `brms` model says the same thing in its own
terms: the `stimulus` slope by item multiplies a predictor that is 0 on every
trial with a new item. In a design in which some items are never old, their
effects on `d` stay at the prior. With `bias` instead of `criterion`, `d` also
moves the criterion and enters every trial.

## Aggregated counts

Item terms need trial rows, because counts summed over a participant's items
no longer say which item each response came from. The same holds for predictors
that change from trial to trial. Without item terms or trial-level predictors,
you do not need trial rows. `sdt_yn()` also takes one row per participant and
stimulus type, with the number of "old" responses and the number of trials.
This layout is faster, because the time a fit takes grows with the number of
rows: here, `r 2 * n_id` rows instead of `r nrow(rec)`.

```{r glmm-agg-fit, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
rec_counts <- aggregate(
  cbind(n_old = resp, n_trials = 1) ~ id + stimulus,
  data = rec, FUN = sum
)
agg_fit <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(d ~ 1 + (1 | id), criterion ~ 1 + (1 | id)),
  data = rec_counts,
  model = sdt_yn(response = "n_old", stimulus = "stimulus",
                 n_trials = "n_trials"),
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  seed = 646,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "fits/bmmfit_sdt_agg_brms_to_bmm"
)
```

For this model, the `r nrow(rec)` trials and the `r nrow(rec_counts)` counts give the same posterior,
because the counts keep everything the trials say about the parameters. To
check this, we take every posterior draw of `agg_fit` and compute two
log-likelihoods: that of the `r nrow(rec)` trial rows, each written as a count of
0 or 1 out of 1 trial, and that of the `r nrow(rec_counts)` counts. Their
difference, the gap, is printed as its range over all draws. If the gap is the
same in every draw, the two log-likelihoods are the same function of the
parameters up to a constant, and with the same priors they give the same
posterior. The second line computes the constant we expect:

```{r glmm-agg-loglik}
rec_single <- transform(rec, n_old = resp, n_trials = 1)
loglik_gap <- rowSums(log_lik(agg_fit, newdata = rec_single)) -
  rowSums(log_lik(agg_fit))
range(loglik_gap)
-sum(lchoose(rec_counts$n_trials, rec_counts$n_old))
```

The gap is the same in every draw, up to rounding, and equals minus the sum of
the log binomial coefficients of the counts. That term does not depend on any
parameter, so it drops out of the posterior.

## Running and comparing trial-level fits

Trial-level fits take longer because they evaluate the likelihood of every
trial. With `backend = "cmdstanr"`, `bmm(..., threads = threading(4))`
evaluates it on four threads in each chain, which shortens the fit if your
machine has cores to spare beyond the chains. `threading()` is the `brms`
function that sets this up, and `threads = 4` is short for it.

`loo()` on a trial-level fit leaves out one trial at a time; on the aggregated
fit, it leaves out one count, that is, all trials of a participant and stimulus
type at once. These are different predictions, so compare the `loo()` results
only between fits to the same rows. To compare a trial-level fit with an
aggregated one, use `kfold(fit, group = "id")`, which leaves out whole
participants in either layout.

# One formula per parameter

Because the response lives in the model object, a `bmmformula` is a list of
regressions, one for each parameter of the model. Each one is a regular `brms`
formula, with population-level effects, group-level effects in the `lme4`
syntax, and non-linear terms if you need them. The
[bmmformula article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_bmmformula.html)
covers the syntax in full, including how to fix a parameter to a constant.

## `0 + setsize` or `1 + setsize`

Most `bmm` articles write `0 + setsize`, and you may be used to `1 + setsize`
(or just `setsize`, which is the same thing). Both describe the same regression
of each parameter on set size. They differ in what each coefficient means, and,
as we show below, in which default prior each coefficient gets.

With `0 + setsize`, the formula has no intercept, and there is one coefficient
per set size. Each coefficient is the parameter in that cell of the design:
`kappa_setsize1` is `kappa` at set size 1, `kappa_setsize6` is `kappa` at set
size 6, both on the log scale explained
[below](#which-scale-the-estimates-are-on). This is often easier when you start
out, because the summary shows the estimate for each condition directly, and
those are the numbers you want to plot or report. If you are not sure which
coding to use, start with this one.

With `1 + setsize`, the intercept is the parameter in the reference condition,
set size 1, and the other coefficients are differences from it.
`kappa_setsize6` is now how much log `kappa` at set size 6 differs from log
`kappa` at set size 1.
This coding is just as suitable, and it reads naturally when the difference
between conditions is your question. To get the parameter in a cell, you add
the coefficients:

```{r bmm-fit-ref, results = "hide", message = FALSE}
bmm_fit_ref <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    kappa ~ 1 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    thetat ~ 1 + setsize + (1 | subID)
  ),
  data = dat,
  model = mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error"),
  cores = 4,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  file = "assets/bmmfit_brms_to_bmm_reference"
)
```

```{r}
fixef(bmm_fit_ref)[c("kappa_Intercept", "kappa_setsize6"), ]

draws_ref <- as_draws_df(bmm_fit_ref)
draws_cell <- as_draws_df(bmm_fit)
kappa6_ref <- draws_ref$b_kappa_Intercept + draws_ref$b_kappa_setsize6
kappa6_cell <- draws_cell$b_kappa_setsize6
rbind(
  `1 + setsize` = quantile(kappa6_ref, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  `0 + setsize` = quantile(kappa6_cell, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
)
```

Add the coefficients draw by draw, as above, and summarize afterwards. The draws
carry the uncertainty of each coefficient and how the coefficients covary, which
adding the two point estimates loses. The reverse also works: a difference
between set sizes is the difference of two cell coefficients of the
`0 + setsize` fit, again taken per draw.

Doing this by hand for every cell and parameter gets tedious.
`native_parameters()` does it for you. It evaluates every parameter in every
cell of the design, whatever the coding of the formula, and reports it on the
scale of the model (more on scales in the next section). Here are both fits
side by side:

```{r}
np_cell <- native_parameters(bmm_fit, re_formula = NA, summary = TRUE)
np_ref <- native_parameters(bmm_fit_ref, re_formula = NA, summary = TRUE)
fmt <- function(np) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", np$Estimate, np$Q2.5, np$Q97.5)
np_cell <- np_cell[np_cell$parameter %in% c("kappa", "thetat"), ]
np_ref <- np_ref[np_ref$parameter %in% c("kappa", "thetat"), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  parameter = np_cell$parameter,
  set_size = np_cell$setsize,
  `0 + setsize` = fmt(np_cell),
  `1 + setsize` = fmt(np_ref[match(paste(np_cell$parameter, np_cell$setsize),
                                   paste(np_ref$parameter, np_ref$setsize)), ]),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE)
```

Unlike the coefficients in the first table, these values are on the scale of
the model: `kappa` is the precision itself, not its log, and `thetat` is shown
as the probability of a memory response, not its logit. `re_formula = NA` sets
the participant effects to zero, which gives the parameters of a typical
participant; `?native_parameters` explains how this differs from the population
average under a non-identity link.

```{r, include = FALSE}
np_ref_matched <- np_ref[match(paste(np_cell$parameter, np_cell$setsize),
                               paste(np_ref$parameter, np_ref$setsize)), ]
rel_diff <- abs(np_ref_matched$Estimate / np_cell$Estimate - 1)
worst <- which.max(rel_diff)
dpr <- mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error")$default_priors
prior_mean <- function(p) as.numeric(sub("^\\w+\\(([-0-9.]+),.*$", "\\1", p))
prior_sd <- function(p) as.numeric(sub("^.*,\\s*([0-9.]+)\\)$", "\\1", p))
kappa_sds <- c(prior_sd(dpr$kappa$main), prior_sd(dpr$kappa$effects))
kappa_cell_prior <- sprintf(
  "normal(%g, %.2f)", prior_mean(dpr$kappa$main), sqrt(sum(kappa_sds^2))
)
kappa_prior_95 <- exp(qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975), prior_mean(dpr$kappa$main),
                            prior_sd(dpr$kappa$main)))
# the brms chunk hard-codes these defaults, the priors section calls the thetat
# prior flat on the probability scale, and kappa_prior_95 assumes a normal
brms_chunk_priors <- c("normal(2, 1)", "logistic(0, 1)",
                       "exponential(1)", "exponential(1)")
if (!identical(c(dpr$kappa$main, dpr$thetat$main, dpr$kappa$sd, dpr$thetat$sd),
               brms_chunk_priors)) {
  stop("The mixture2p default priors changed: revise the brms chunk and the ",
       "priors section.")
}
thetat_cell1 <- c(mean(draws_cell$b_thetat_setsize1),
                  mean(draws_ref$b_thetat_Intercept))
thetat_diff_gap <- max(abs(vapply(set_sizes[-1], function(s) {
  mean(draws_cell[[paste0("b_thetat_setsize", s)]] - draws_cell$b_thetat_setsize1) -
    mean(draws_ref[[paste0("b_thetat_setsize", s)]])
}, numeric(1))))
```

On the scale of the model, the two codings give practically the same estimates.
In every cell, the estimates of the two fits differ by less than
`r ceiling(max(rel_diff) * 1000) / 10`% of the `0 + setsize` estimate; the
largest gap is `r np_cell$parameter[worst]` at set size
`r np_cell$setsize[worst]`, `r sprintf("%.2f", np_cell$Estimate[worst])` against
`r sprintf("%.2f", np_ref_matched$Estimate[worst])`. Pick the coding whose
coefficients you want to read.

What the coding does change is the default prior of each coefficient. `bmm`
sets its default priors per coefficient, and the value of a parameter in one
cell is a different quantity from the difference between two cells: the first
lies somewhere in the plausible range of the parameter, the second is centered
on zero. With `0 + setsize`, every coefficient is a cell, so every one gets the
prior for the parameter itself, `r dpr$kappa$main` for `kappa` on the log scale
and `r dpr$thetat$main` for `thetat`. With `1 + setsize`, only the intercept,
the reference cell, gets that prior. The differences get the prior for effects,
`r dpr$kappa$effects` for `kappa` and `r dpr$thetat$effects` for `thetat`. Any
other cell is the intercept plus a difference, so its prior is that of a sum of
two independent coefficients. For `kappa`, the two normal priors add up to
`r kappa_cell_prior`, whose standard deviation is the square root of
`r kappa_sds[1]`² + `r kappa_sds[2]`²: wider than the `r dpr$kappa$main` that
the same cell gets with `0 + setsize`. With this data set, the table above shows
that the difference barely matters. The table hides one exception, visible only
on the logit scale: `thetat` at set size 1. Near a probability of 1, the data
say little about the logit, and with `1 + setsize` the effects prior, centered
on zero, pulls the reference cell towards the other set sizes. On the logit
scale, the two fits estimate `thetat` at set size 1 as
`r sprintf("%.2f", thetat_cell1[1])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", thetat_cell1[2])`,
and the set-size differences of `thetat` differ by up to
`r sprintf("%.2f", thetat_diff_gap)` logits. With fewer trials per cell, the
priors carry more weight, and the two codings can give different estimates. So
check `default_prior()` for the coding you use, as shown in [the section on
priors](#why-the-default-priors-are-informative), and set your own priors if the
defaults do not match what you know.

The participant effects can be coded either way, too. `(1 | subID)`, as here,
gives every participant one shift for all set sizes. `(0 + setsize | subID)` and
`(1 + setsize | subID)` both let participants differ per set size, coded as cell
values or as differences from the reference cell.

# Which scale the estimates are on

The summary of a `bmm` fit lists the link of each parameter:

```{r, comment = NA}
summary(bmm_fit)
```

`kappa` must be positive, and `thetat` turns into a probability. Neither can be
predicted by a linear model directly, so `bmm` estimates them on an unbounded
scale and transforms them back. `kappa` has a log link, so the coefficients are
log precisions. `thetat` has a logit link. `brms` fixes the weight of the
second, guessing component (`theta2`) at 0 on this scale, so a `thetat` of 0
means that memory and guessing are equally likely, and the probability that a
response comes from memory is `plogis(thetat)`. Every coefficient in the
summary, every prior, and every value you fix a parameter to lives on this link
scale.

To report a parameter on its own scale, transform the draws and summarize
afterwards, not the other way around. The mean of `exp()` of the draws is not
`exp()` of their mean. For set size 6:

```{r}
c(
  `exp(mean)` = exp(mean(kappa6_cell)),
  `mean(exp)` = mean(exp(kappa6_cell))
)
```

`native_parameters()`, used above, follows this order for every parameter. For
the mixture models, `k2sd()` converts `kappa` into the circular standard
deviation in radians, which is the measure of precision many papers report:

```{r}
kappa_draws <- native_parameters(bmm_fit, re_formula = NA, pars = "kappa")
sd_deg <- k2sd(kappa_draws$value) * 180 / pi
tapply(sd_deg, kappa_draws$setsize, median)
```

A coefficient on its own transforms to something else. With `1 + setsize`,
`exp(b_kappa_setsize6)` is the factor by which `kappa` at set size 6 is larger
or smaller than at set size 1, not `kappa` at set size 6. The help page of each
model lists the links of its parameters.

# Why the default priors are informative

`brms` uses flat priors on regression coefficients unless you set them. For the
`brms` version of this model, the defaults are:

```{r}
default_prior(
  bf(
    response_error ~ 1,
    kappa1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    theta1 ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID),
    mu2 ~ 1,
    kappa2 ~ 1
  ),
  data = dat,
  family = mixture(von_mises, von_mises, order = "none")
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  transform(prior = ifelse(prior == "", "(flat)", prior)) |>
  subset(dpar %in% c("kappa1", "theta1") & coef == "" & group == "",
         select = c(dpar, class, prior)) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

`class = b` covers every coefficient of `kappa1` and `theta1`, so each of them
has a flat prior. That suits a regression whose coefficients could take any
value. It does not suit a measurement model. Its parameters stand for cognitive
processes, and we know roughly which values are plausible before seeing any data. `bmm` puts this
knowledge into its default priors:

```{r}
default_prior(
  bmf(kappa ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID), thetat ~ 0 + setsize + (1 | subID)),
  data = dat,
  model = mixture2p(resp_error = "response_error")
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  subset(dpar %in% c("kappa", "thetat") & coef == "" & group == "",
         select = c(dpar, class, prior)) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

The `r dpr$kappa$main` on the log of `kappa` places 95% of its mass between a
`kappa` of `r sprintf("%.1f", kappa_prior_95[1])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", kappa_prior_95[2])`,
that is, between a circular standard deviation of
`r round(k2sd(kappa_prior_95[1]) * 180 / pi)` and
`r round(k2sd(kappa_prior_95[2]) * 180 / pi)` degrees. Values in the thousands,
which would mean a circular standard deviation of
`r round(k2sd(1000) * 180 / pi, 1)` degrees or less, get next to no prior mass.
The `r dpr$thetat$main` on `thetat` is flat on the probability scale: before
seeing the data, every probability of a memory response between 0 and 1 is
equally likely. It still does work that the `brms` default does not: a flat
prior on the logit is improper and, on the probability scale, piles its mass at
0 and 1.

There is a second reason, which has to do with the mixture. When `kappa` comes
close to 0, the memory distribution becomes as flat as the guessing
distribution, and the data cannot tell the two apart. In that region, `thetat`
can take any value without changing the fit. A flat prior does nothing to keep
the sampler out of that region; a prior that holds `kappa` in a plausible range
does.

What this means for you:

- The more trials per participant and condition, the less the estimates
  depend on the priors. With few trials, the priors pull the estimates towards
  their center.
- Look at the priors before you fit, with `default_prior()` as above, and at
  the help page of the model, which lists them.
- If you know more than the defaults, or something different, set your own
  priors with `prior = ` in `bmm()`. They are `brms` priors on the `bmm`
  parameter names, with `nlpar` or `dpar` as `default_prior()` shows it, for
  example `prior(normal(1.5, 0.5), class = b, nlpar = kappa)`, again on the log
  scale. With `0 + setsize`, this sets the prior of every cell of `kappa`. With
  `1 + setsize`, it sets the prior of the differences only; the intercept takes
  `coef = "Intercept"`, as `default_prior()` shows for that coding. The
  [article on extracting model information](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_extract_info.html)
  shows the details.
- Bayes factors depend on the priors much more than estimates do. If you plan to
  compute them, choose the priors on purpose rather than taking the defaults.

# What stays brms

A `bmm` fit is a `brmsfit` with extra information, so the `brms` toolbox works
on it: `fixef()`, `ranef()`, `as_draws_df()`, `pp_check()`,
`conditional_effects()`, `hypothesis()`, `loo()` and the rest. As shown above,
`bmm_fit$formula` holds the `brmsformula` that `bmm` generated, and
`stancode(bmm_fit)` the Stan code. `summary(bmm_fit, backend = "brms")` prints
the `brms` summary instead of the `bmm` one. It lists the link of `theta1` as
`identity`, because `brms` applies the softmax inside the mixture family. If you
want to change a model beyond what `bmm` offers, these give you the `brms` code to start from.
